This notebook relates nutrient concentrations and water quality (PC1,
[D14](D14-nutrient-impact-presence.qmd)) to their drivers: land cover, climate
and the weather of the year. The link between these drivers, nutrients and
fish (species presence, food web structure) will be the subject of a later
notebook.

The notebook starts by getting and presenting the driver data, from their
original sources:

- the **catchment** of each station, i.e. the area draining to the station,
computed from the [HydroSHEDS](https://www.hydrosheds.org/) flow directions
- the **land cover** of the catchment, from [CORINE Land
Cover](https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/corine-land-cover)
- the **weather** of the catchment, year by year, from
[WorldClim](https://worldclim.org/)

and then models the nutrient concentrations on these drivers.

## Setup

```{r setup}
library(renv)
renv::load()
library(targets)
library(here)
tar_config_set(
  store = here::here("_targets")
)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
devtools::load_all()
nice_theme()
```

We study the NAIADES stations having a water quality index (PC1, D14) and
fish visits, i.e. the stations whose Sandre code is the site of a fish visit
of D12 (target `water_quality_visit`).

```{r data}
station <- tar_read(naiades_station)
water_quality <- tar_read(water_quality)
fish_station <- unique(tar_read(water_quality_visit)$code_station)
district <- tar_read(basin) |>
  filter(district %in% tar_read(params)$district_kept)
direction <- terra::rast(tar_read(flow_direction_file))
station_flow <- tar_read(station_flow) |>
  mutate(
    matched = abs(log(area / rht_area)) < log(1.5),
    studied = code_station %in% water_quality$code_station & code_station %in% fish_station
  )
```

## Catchments

### Flow directions

HydroSHEDS [@Lehner-Verdin-Jarvis-2008] describes where water flows, and it
is computed from the elevation of the land only. It does not observe water:
it assumes that rain falls everywhere and that water always goes downhill.
The idea is illustrated below on a synthetic grid.

1. **Elevation.** The land is cut into a grid of cells (15 arc-seconds, about
   450 m × 310 m in France), each with an elevation measured from space.
2. **Flow direction.** From each cell, water goes to the lowest of its 8
   neighbours. This gives one arrow per cell, everywhere, whether there is a
river or not. This grid of flow direction is the data provided by HydroSHEDS.
3. **Rivers.** Drainage area can be reconstructed from flow directions. Counting
   for each cell how many cells drain through it (or rather summing their area)
gives its upstream area. In other words, a river is simply a cell with a large
upstream area: in valley bottoms, the water of a large area passes through.
4. **Catchment.** The catchment of a cell is the set of cells whose arrows
   eventually lead to it, i.e. the area whose water passes through that cell.

```{r flow-toy}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
toy <- terra::rast(
  outer(7:1, c(4, 2, 0, 1, 3), \(r, c) 3 * r + 2 * c) + c(0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1),
  extent = terra::ext(0, 5, 0, 7)
)
toy_direction <- terra::terrain(toy, "flowdir")
toy_angle <- c(`1` = 0, `2` = -45, `4` = -90, `8` = -135, `16` = 180, `32` = 135, `64` = 90, `128` = 45)
toy_df <- as.data.frame(c(toy, toy_direction, terra::flowAccumulation(toy_direction)), xy = TRUE) |>
  setNames(c("x", "y", "elevation", "direction", "cells")) |>
  mutate(
    angle = toy_angle[as.character(direction)] * pi / 180,
    xend = x + 0.35 * cos(angle), yend = y + 0.35 * sin(angle)
  )
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  ggplot(toy_df, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_tile(aes(fill = elevation), colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = elevation), size = 3.5) +
    scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlOrBr", direction = 1, guide = "none") +
    coord_equal() +
    theme_void() +
    labs(title = "1. Elevation (m)"),
  ggplot(toy_df, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_tile(fill = "grey95", colour = "white") +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = xend, yend = yend), arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")), na.rm = TRUE) +
    coord_equal() +
    theme_void() +
    labs(title = "2. Flow direction"),
  ggplot(toy_df, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_tile(aes(fill = cells >= 5), colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = cells), size = 3.5) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c(`TRUE` = "steelblue", `FALSE` = "grey95"),
      labels = c(`TRUE` = "river (5 cells or more)", `FALSE` = "no river"), name = NULL
    ) +
    coord_equal() +
    theme_void() +
    labs(title = "3. Cells draining through"),
  nrow = 1
)
```

In this made-up valley, the water of the slopes flows to the valley bottom
(middle column) and then down to the outlet (bottom, where the water leaves
the grid); the cells of the valley bottom collect the water of many cells and
form the river. The catchment of the outlet is the whole grid.

The measured elevation has errors, and some structures (bridges, dams,
embankments) look like obstacles across the valleys. HydroSHEDS
corrects the elevation with existing maps of rivers and lakes, so that the
computed rivers follow the real ones.

Summing a value over the catchment of every cell at once is called flow
accumulation (`terra::flowAccumulation()`). It gives the upstream area of each
cell (left map, only the cells draining more than 50 km²); we will later use the
same computation later to average land cover and weather over the catchments.

```{r upstream-map}
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 8
upstream <- terra::flowAccumulation(direction, weight = terra::cellSize(direction, unit = "km"))
upstream_df <- as.data.frame(upstream, xy = TRUE) |>
  setNames(c("x", "y", "area")) |>
  filter(area > 50)
# flow direction and upstream area of the cells of a window, with arrows
flow_arrow <- function(window) {
  window <- terra::align(window, direction, snap = "out")
  angle <- c(`1` = 0, `2` = -45, `4` = -90, `8` = -135, `16` = 180, `32` = 135, `64` = 90, `128` = 45)
  step <- 0.35 * terra::res(direction)[1]
  terra::crop(c(direction, upstream), window) |>
    as.data.frame(xy = TRUE) |>
    setNames(c("x", "y", "code", "area")) |>
    mutate(
      angle = angle[as.character(code)] * pi / 180,
      xend = x + step * cos(angle), yend = y + step * sin(angle)
    )
}
zoom <- terra::ext(2.71, 2.86, 43.65, 43.75)
zoom_df <- flow_arrow(zoom)
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  ggplot() +
    geom_raster(
      aes(x, y, fill = area),
      data = as.data.frame(terra::mask(upstream, terra::vect(district)), xy = TRUE) |>
        setNames(c("x", "y", "area")) |>
        filter(area > 50)
    ) +
    geom_sf(data = district, fill = NA, colour = "grey40") +
    annotate(
      "rect", xmin = zoom$xmin, xmax = zoom$xmax, ymin = zoom$ymin, ymax = zoom$ymax,
      fill = NA, colour = "red", linewidth = 1
    ) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", option = "mako", direction = -1, end = 0.75, name = "Upstream area (km²)") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "1. Upstream area") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm")),
  ggplot(zoom_df) +
    geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = area)) +
    geom_segment(
      aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3,
      arrow = arrow(length = unit(1, "mm")), na.rm = TRUE
    ) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", option = "mako", direction = -1, name = "Upstream area (km²)") +
    coord_sf(expand = FALSE) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "2. Zoom: flow direction and upstream area") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm")),
  nrow = 1
)
```

The next step is to snap our stations to this flow lines, so we can get their
catchment area.

### Snapping stations

The HydroSHEDS grid is relatively coarse. So it happens that the river often
passes one or two cells away from the station. Then, we move each station to the
cell, within 1 km, whose upstream area is closest to the drained area of the
nearest reach of the RHT (@Pella-etal-2012). Stations whose upstream area is
still more than 1.5 times larger or smaller than the RHT area (outside the
blue band below) are considered unmatched (target `station_flow`).

```{r snapping}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
station_flow |>
  filter(studied) |>
  ggplot(aes(rht_area, area, colour = matched)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(x, ymin = x / 1.5, ymax = x * 1.5),
    data = tibble(x = 10^seq(0, log10(max(station_flow$rht_area[station_flow$studied])), length.out = 100)),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey30", `FALSE` = "firebrick"), name = "Matched") +
  labs(x = "RHT drained area (km²)", y = "HydroSHEDS upstream area (km²)")
station_flow |>
  filter(studied) |>
  summarise(
    stations = n(), matched = sum(matched), `matched (%)` = round(100 * sum(matched) / n()),
    `median area (km²)` = median(area[matched])
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Most stations are snapped correctly, we only leave out 5% of the stations which
we consider to be satisfying. 

Now that we have our stations snapped to the HydroSHEDS flow cells we can
compute their catchment. We illustrate this below.

### Example catchments

The catchment of a station is drawn by following the flow directions upstream
(`terra::watershed()`). To illustrate, we plot three stations and their
catchment with different draining area below.

```{r catchment-example}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
example <- purrr::map_dfr(c(20, 300, 3000), \(size) {
  station_flow |>
    filter(matched, studied) |>
    slice_min(abs(log(area / size)), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
})
draw_catchment <- function(example) {
  watershed <- terra::watershed(direction, pourpoint = cbind(example$longitude, example$latitude))
  terra::as.polygons(terra::ifel(watershed == 1, 1, NA)) |>
    st_as_sf() |>
    mutate(code_station = example$code_station, area = example$area)
}
catchment <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(example)), \(i) draw_catchment(example[i, ]))
plot_catchment <- function(i) {
  frame <- st_bbox(st_buffer(catchment[i, ], 2000))
  stream <- upstream_df |>
    filter(between(x, frame["xmin"], frame["xmax"]), between(y, frame["ymin"], frame["ymax"]))
  plot <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = catchment[i, ], fill = "lightblue", colour = "steelblue") +
    geom_raster(aes(x, y, alpha = log10(area)), data = stream, fill = "navy", show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_point(aes(longitude, latitude), data = example[i, ], colour = "red", size = 2) +
    coord_sf(xlim = frame[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = frame[c("ymin", "ymax")]) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = sprintf("%s, %.0f km²", example$code_station[i], example$area[i]))
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(lapply(seq_len(nrow(example)), plot_catchment), nrow = 1)
```

These catchments are useful because from them we can get the land use or climate
that is affecting any given stations. We derive this environmental information
in what follows.

## Land cover

### CORINE Land Cover

CORINE Land Cover maps land cover using satellite images (Landsat). A mapping
unit is a polygon of at least 25 ha. A vintage is one edition of the map, for a
reference year: we use the 2000, 2006, 2012 and 2018 vintages for mainland
France. Each vintage also comes with a layer of the changes since the previous
vintage, mapped with a finer unit of 5 ha.

Next, we dive into the nomenclature of the database which is used to classify
the different land-uses.

#### Nomenclature

There are 3 different levels of classifications, from finer to coarser

- level 3 has 44 classes;
- level 2 has 15 classes;
- level 1 has 5 classes.

For sake of simplicity, we present the data at level 1, which is enough to
describe the landscape. For the models, we split the agricultural areas into
**arable land** (level 2 class 21) and **other farmland** (classes 22-24:
permanent pastures, vineyards and orchards), since they act differently
on nitrate.

These five groups are used for the catchments:

```{r corine-nomenclature}
corine_class <- tibble::tribble(
  ~class, ~name, ~group, ~colour,
  11, "Urban fabric", "Artificial", "#e6004d",
  12, "Industrial, commercial and transport units", "Artificial", "#cc4df2",
  13, "Mine, dump and construction sites", "Artificial", "#a600cc",
  14, "Artificial, non-agricultural vegetated areas", "Artificial", "#ffa6ff",
  21, "Arable land", "Agricultural", "#ffffa8",
  22, "Permanent crops (vineyards, orchards)", "Agricultural", "#e68000",
  23, "Pastures", "Agricultural", "#e6e64d",
  24, "Heterogeneous agricultural areas", "Agricultural", "#ffe6a6",
  31, "Forests", "Forest and semi-natural", "#00a600",
  32, "Scrub and herbaceous vegetation", "Forest and semi-natural", "#a6f200",
  33, "Open spaces with little or no vegetation", "Forest and semi-natural", "#e6e6e6",
  41, "Inland wetlands", "Wetlands", "#a6a6ff",
  42, "Maritime wetlands", "Wetlands", "#ccccff",
  51, "Inland waters", "Water bodies", "#80f2e6",
  52, "Marine waters", "Water bodies", "#e6f2ff"
) |>
  mutate(category = case_when(
    group == "Agricultural" & class == 21 ~ "Arable land",
    group == "Agricultural" ~ "Other farmland",
    group %in% c("Wetlands", "Water bodies") ~ "Wetlands and water",
    .default = group
  ))
corine_colour <- setNames(corine_class$colour, corine_class$name)
group_colour <- c(
  "Artificial" = "#e6004d", "Agricultural" = "#ffd84d", "Forest and semi-natural" = "#2e8b3a",
  "Wetlands" = "#a6a6ff", "Water bodies" = "#4da6ff"
)
category_colour <- c(
  "Artificial" = "#e6004d", "Arable land" = "#ffd84d", "Other farmland" = "#b8c95b",
  "Forest and semi-natural" = "#2e8b3a", "Wetlands and water" = "#4da6ff"
)
corine_code <- tibble::tribble(
  ~code, ~code_name,
  111, "Continuous urban fabric", 112, "Discontinuous urban fabric",
  121, "Industrial or commercial units", 122, "Road and rail networks", 123, "Port areas",
  124, "Airports", 131, "Mineral extraction sites", 132, "Dump sites", 133, "Construction sites",
  141, "Green urban areas", 142, "Sport and leisure facilities",
  211, "Non-irrigated arable land", 212, "Permanently irrigated land", 213, "Rice fields",
  221, "Vineyards", 222, "Fruit trees and berry plantations", 223, "Olive groves",
  231, "Pastures", 241, "Annual crops associated with permanent crops",
  242, "Complex cultivation patterns",
  243, "Agriculture with significant areas of natural vegetation", 244, "Agro-forestry areas",
  311, "Broad-leaved forest", 312, "Coniferous forest", 313, "Mixed forest",
  321, "Natural grasslands", 322, "Moors and heathland", 323, "Sclerophyllous vegetation",
  324, "Transitional woodland-shrub", 331, "Beaches, dunes, sands", 332, "Bare rocks",
  333, "Sparsely vegetated areas", 334, "Burnt areas", 335, "Glaciers and perpetual snow",
  411, "Inland marshes", 412, "Peat bogs", 421, "Salt marshes", 422, "Salines",
  423, "Intertidal flats", 511, "Water courses", 512, "Water bodies", 521, "Coastal lagoons",
  522, "Estuaries", 523, "Sea and ocean"
) |>
  mutate(class = code %/% 10)
knitr::kable(
  select(corine_class, group, class, name, category),
  col.names = c("Level 1", "Code", "Level 2", "Group used for the catchments")
)
```

Next, we look at the spatial unit used in the database, that is the polygons.

#### Polygons

Number and size of the polygons of each vintage (sea excluded):

```{r corine-polygon}
corine_polygon <- tar_read(corine_polygon) |>
  filter(code != 523)
corine_polygon |>
  summarise(
    polygons = n(), `median area (ha)` = median(area),
    `polygons < 25 ha (%)` = 100 * mean(area < 24.5),
    `total area (km²)` = sum(area) / 100,
    .by = year
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

And the distribution of polygon areas.

```{r corine-polygon-size}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
corine_polygon |>
  filter(year == 2018) |>
  ggplot(aes(area)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 25, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 25, 100, 1000, 1e4, 1e5, 1e6), labels = scales::label_comma(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Polygon area (ha), CORINE 2018", y = "Polygons")
```

The few polygons under 25 ha are cut by the national border or the coast. The
largest ones are forests and mountain areas of thousands of hectares.

Now that we have investigate the polygon we can have a look at the map.

#### Map

Here is the map of land-uses (level 1 classes, for 2018).

```{r corine-map}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
corine_map <- terra::rast(tar_read(corine_map_file))
corine_map <- terra::mask(terra::crop(corine_map, terra::vect(district)), terra::vect(district))
as.data.frame(corine_map, xy = TRUE) |>
  setNames(c("x", "y", "code")) |>
  filter(!is.na(code), code > 0, code != 523) |>
  mutate(class = code %/% 10) |>
  left_join(corine_class, by = "class") |>
  mutate(group = factor(group, names(group_colour))) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = group)) +
  geom_sf(data = district, fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colour, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Agricultural areas cover most of the four districts. Forests
and semi-natural areas form large blocks, and artificial areas are small spots
except Paris.

We can also plot the share of the different classes across the years.

```{r corine-area}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
corine_area <- corine_polygon |>
  mutate(class = code %/% 10) |>
  summarise(area = sum(area), .by = c(year, class)) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * area / sum(area), .by = year) |>
  left_join(corine_class, by = "class")
corine_area |>
  summarise(share = sum(share), .by = c(year, group)) |>
  mutate(group = forcats::fct_reorder(group, share, mean)) |>
  ggplot(aes(share, group, fill = factor(year))) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(reverse = TRUE)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(5, "Blues")[-1], name = "Vintage") +
  labs(x = "Share of mainland France (%)", y = NULL)
```

Agricultural land dominates land uses. Overall, the share of land-uses doesn't
change much over the years. We mainly notice an increase of artificial areas.

### Land cover of the catchments

For each vintage, we rasterise the CORINE polygons (level-2 classes) on the
flow-direction grid, such that for each cell we have the fraction of covered by
the class. The share of a class in the catchment of a station is the flow
accumulation of the class area divided by the total flow accumulation.

We illustrate this with an example below.

```{r landcover}
landcover <- tar_read(station_landcover) |>
  semi_join(filter(station_flow, matched, studied), by = "code_station") |>
  left_join(corine_class, by = "class")
```

We perform the following steps:

1. we keep the polygons intersecting the catchment;
2. the polygons are rasterised on a grid 5 times finer than the flow-direction
   grid, and the fraction of each flow cell covered by each land cover class is
computed;
3. the share of each class in the catchment is the mean of these fractions over
   the cells of the catchment, weighted by cell area. Flow accumulation computes
this mean for all the cells of the grid at once.

```{r landcover-example}
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5.5
corine_zip <- tar_read(corine_zip)
example_station <- example[2, ]
example_catchment <- catchment[2, ]
example_window <- terra::align(terra::ext(terra::vect(st_buffer(example_catchment, 2000))), direction, snap = "out")
example_watershed <- terra::crop(
  terra::watershed(direction, pourpoint = cbind(example_station$longitude, example_station$latitude)),
  example_window
)
# 1. polygons cut along the catchment
example_polygon <- read_corine(corine_zip[grepl("2018", corine_zip)], example_catchment) |>
  st_intersection(st_transform(st_geometry(example_catchment), 2154)) |>
  mutate(class = code %/% 10) |>
  left_join(corine_class, by = "class")
# 2. fraction of arable land in each flow-direction cell
example_fine <- rasterize_corine(
  corine_zip[grepl("2018", corine_zip)], as.vector(example_window), terra::res(direction)[1] / 5,
  tempfile(fileext = ".tif")
)
example_cover <- terra::aggregate(terra::rast(example_fine) %/% 10 == 21, 5, mean)
example_cell <- c(example_cover, example_watershed) |>
  as.data.frame(xy = TRUE) |>
  setNames(c("x", "y", "arable", "inside")) |>
  filter(inside == 1)
# 3. shares in the catchment
example_share <- landcover |>
  filter(code_station == example_station$code_station, year == 2018) |>
  summarise(share = sum(share), .by = category) |>
  filter(share > 0)
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = category), data = example_polygon, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_sf(data = example_catchment, fill = NA, colour = "black") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = category_colour) +
    labs(title = "1. CORINE polygons"),
  ggplot() +
    geom_tile(aes(x, y, fill = 100 * arable), data = example_cell) +
    geom_sf(data = example_catchment, fill = NA, colour = "black") +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "goldenrod3", name = "Arable\nland (%)") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "2. Arable fraction of each cell"),
  example_share |>
    mutate(category = forcats::fct_reorder(category, share, max)) |>
    ggplot(aes(share, category, fill = category)) +
    geom_col(colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = category_colour) +
    labs(x = "Share of the catchment (%)", y = NULL, title = "3. Shares in the catchment"),
  nrow = 1, widths = c(1, 1, 1.2)
)
```

We can do this for all station catchments to have an overview of the data.

```{r landcover-distribution}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
landcover |>
  filter(year == 2018) |>
  summarise(share = sum(share), .by = c(code_station, category)) |>
  mutate(category = factor(category, rev(names(category_colour)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(share, category, fill = category)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.2, outlier.alpha = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = category_colour) +
  labs(x = "Share of the catchment (%), 2018", y = NULL)
```

We retrieve that farmland and arable dominates, followed by natural and
artificial areas.

Next, we have a look at the weather data from WorldClim.

## Weather

### WorldClim

WorldClim historical monthly weather gives, for each month from 1950 to 2021,
the precipitation and the means of the daily minimum and maximum temperature,
on a 2.5 arc-minute grid (about 4.5 km). Each monthly value combines two
sources:

- a **baseline**, constant in time: the WorldClim 1970-2000 average of the
  calendar month [@Fick-Hijmans-2017], interpolated at fine resolution from
  many weather stations, elevation and satellite data. It carries the spatial
  detail (relief, rain shadows);
- a **departure** from this baseline: how much the month differs from its
  1970-2000 average in CRU TS [@Harris-etal-2020], a coarser interpolation
  of weather stations on a 0.5° grid (about 50 km). It carries the variation
  between years, and is added to the baseline for temperature and multiplied
  with it for precipitation.

So the differences between places are well resolved, but the year-to-year
variation is smooth over about 50 km: nearby catchments get almost the same
weather anomaly in a given year. We keep 2000-2021 (target `worldclim_file`)
and summarise each year by the annual precipitation, the annual mean
temperature and the summer (June-August) mean of the daily maximum
temperature.

```{r weather-map}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5
yearly <- summarise_worldclim(tar_read(worldclim_file))
weather_mean <- c(
  terra::mean(yearly[[grepl("^precipitation", names(yearly))]]),
  terra::mean(yearly[[grepl("^temperature", names(yearly))]]),
  terra::mean(yearly[[grepl("^summer_tmax", names(yearly))]])
)
names(weather_mean) <- c("Annual precipitation (mm)", "Annual mean temperature (°C)", "Summer maximum temperature (°C)")
patchwork::wrap_plots(lapply(names(weather_mean), \(v) {
  ggplot() +
    geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = value), data = setNames(as.data.frame(weather_mean[[v]], xy = TRUE), c("x", "y", "value"))) +
    geom_sf(data = district, fill = NA, colour = "grey20") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = if (grepl("precipitation", v)) "mako" else "inferno", direction = if (grepl("precipitation", v)) -1 else 1, name = NULL) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = paste(v, "\n2000-2021"))
}), nrow = 1)
```

Next, we compute the climate information for each catchment-year.

### Weather of the catchments

We proceed as for land cover.

The WorldClim cells are split into the cells of the flow-direction grid (10 ×
10 per WorldClim cell), and the weather of a catchment in a year is the mean
over the catchment, weighted by cell area (target `station_weather`).

```{r weather-year}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
weather <- tar_read(station_weather) |>
  semi_join(filter(station_flow, matched, studied), by = "code_station")
weather |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(precipitation, temperature, summer_tmax)) |>
  summarise(
    low = quantile(value, 0.1), median = median(value), high = quantile(value, 0.9),
    .by = c(name, year)
  ) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, c("precipitation", "temperature", "summer_tmax"), c("Annual precipitation (mm)", "Annual mean temperature (°C)", "Summer maximum temperature (°C)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, median)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Median and 10-90% of the station catchments")
```

We can illustrate this with an example.

```{r weather-example}
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 5
example_frame <- terra::ext(terra::vect(st_buffer(example_catchment, 5000)))
example_weather_map <- terra::crop(weather_mean[[1:2]], example_frame, snap = "out") |>
  as.data.frame(xy = TRUE) |>
  setNames(c("x", "y", "precipitation", "temperature"))
example_year <- tar_read(station_weather) |>
  filter(code_station == example_station$code_station)
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  ggplot() +
    geom_tile(aes(x, y, fill = precipitation), data = example_weather_map, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
    geom_sf(data = example_catchment, fill = NA, colour = "black") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, name = "mm", n.breaks = 4, guide = guide_colourbar(barwidth = 8)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Annual precipitation"),
  ggplot() +
    geom_tile(aes(x, y, fill = temperature), data = example_weather_map, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
    geom_sf(data = example_catchment, fill = NA, colour = "black") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", name = "°C", n.breaks = 4, guide = guide_colourbar(barwidth = 8)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Annual mean temperature"),
  ggplot(example_year, aes(year, precipitation)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = mean(example_year$precipitation), linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Annual precipitation (mm)", title = "Catchment, per year"),
  ggplot(tidyr::pivot_longer(example_year, c(temperature, summer_tmax)), aes(year, value, colour = name)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_point() +
    scale_colour_manual(
      values = c(temperature = "darkorange", summer_tmax = "firebrick"),
      labels = c(temperature = "Annual mean", summer_tmax = "Summer maximum"), name = NULL
    ) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Temperature (°C)", title = "Catchment, per year") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom"),
  nrow = 1
)
```

We are ready to model the drivers effect on nutrients.

## Drivers of nutrients

Correlation between the catchment drivers across stations (2018 land cover,
mean weather 2000-2021, catchment area):

```{r driver-correlation}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
driver <- landcover |>
  filter(year == 2018) |>
  filter(category != "Wetlands and water") |>
  mutate(type = c(
    "Artificial" = "artificial", "Arable land" = "arable", "Other farmland" = "other_farmland",
    "Forest and semi-natural" = "forest_semi_natural"
  )[category]) |>
  summarise(share = sum(share), .by = c(code_station, type)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = share) |>
  inner_join(
    weather |> summarise(across(c(precipitation, temperature, summer_tmax), mean), .by = code_station),
    by = "code_station"
  ) |>
  inner_join(transmute(station_flow, code_station, log_area = log10(area)), by = "code_station")
correlation <- cor(select(driver, -code_station))
as.data.frame(as.table(correlation)) |>
  ggplot(aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Freq)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu", limits = c(-1, 1), direction = 1, name = "r") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

We can start to build the model.

### Model

For each nutrient (log10 station-year mean, see
[D14](D14-nutrient-impact-presence.qmd)) and for the water
quality index PC1, we build a Gaussian model of the standardised response on the
following drivers, all standardised:

- land cover
- climate (mean over 2000-2021)
- weather of the year (anomaly compared to the mean)
- catchment area (for control)

We also add a spatial field (SPDE), an AR1 year effect shared by all stations
(national dry or wet years, trends) and an iid station effect.

```{r driver-data}
driver_data <- tar_read(driver_data)
driver_model <- tar_read(driver_model)
tibble(
  `station-years` = nrow(driver_data),
  stations = n_distinct(driver_data$code_station),
  years = paste(range(driver_data$year), collapse = "-")
) |>
  knitr::kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Next, we run the model and plot the results as a coefplot.

```{r driver-effect}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 7
driver_label <- c(
  arable = "Arable land", other_farmland = "Other farmland", artificial = "Artificial areas", precipitation = "Precipitation", air_temperature = "Air temperature",
  area = "Catchment area",
  precipitation_anomaly = "Precipitation of the year", precipitation_previous = "Precipitation of the previous year",
  temperature_anomaly = "Air temperature of the year"
)
driver_group <- c(
  arable = "Land cover", other_farmland = "Land cover", artificial = "Land cover",
  precipitation = "Climate", air_temperature = "Climate", area = "Catchment",
  precipitation_anomaly = "Weather of the year", precipitation_previous = "Weather of the year",
  temperature_anomaly = "Weather of the year"
)
driver_colour <- c(
  "Land cover" = "#D55E00", "Climate" = "#0072B2", "Weather of the year" = "#009E73", "Catchment" = "grey40"
)
driver_effect <- purrr::map_dfr(driver_model, \(m) {
  tibble::as_tibble(m$summary.fixed, rownames = "term") |>
    filter(term != "Intercept") |>
    transmute(response = m$response, term, mean, low = `0.045quant`, high = `0.955quant`)
}) |>
  mutate(
    credible = sign(low) == sign(high),
    group = factor(driver_group[term], c("Land cover", "Climate", "Weather of the year", "Catchment")),
    term = factor(driver_label[term], rev(driver_label)),
    response = factor(response, c("nitrate", "ammonium", "orthophosphate", "total_phosphorus", "PC1"))
  )
ggplot(driver_effect, aes(mean, term, colour = group, alpha = credible)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high), size = 0.3, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = driver_colour, guide = "none") +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1, `FALSE` = 0.3), guide = "none") +
  facet_grid(group ~ response, scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Effect (SD of the response per SD of the driver, 91% credible interval)", y = NULL) +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0))
```

**Results:**

- **Land cover** is by far the strongest driver. Arable land is the main
source of nitrate, raising it much more than other farmland. Phosphorus
rises as much with other farmland as with arable land, and also with
artificial areas, which are the main source of ammonium. Water quality
(PC1) decreases with all three.
- **Climate:** drier catchments have more nutrients, especially phosphorus,
and warmer catchments too; both have a lower water quality.
- **Weather of the year** has small effects compared with land cover and
climate. Nutrients are slightly higher after a dry year (the flush of what
accumulated during the dry year), and ammonium is lower in warm years.
- **Catchment area** has almost no effect.

## Next steps

- The link with fish (species presence, food web structure) will be studied
in a separate notebook, with a model of the paths from the drivers to fish,
direct or through nutrients.
- Add the presence of dams in the catchment (upstream of the station) as a
driver of the nutrient concentrations and of the water quality: reservoirs
can retain phosphorus and remove nitrogen, or release nutrients and
ammonium when their water is low in oxygen.
